title: The chief end (Westminster Shorter Catechism, 1647)
hook: Q1: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mystery of love: love doesn't explain suffering, but it walks into it. Your line was love enters. Whose hard day did you step into? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

A question and answer, written for teaching. The question: "What is the chief end of man?" Chief end. The main thing a human life is for. You might expect a long answer. Duty, rules, a list of obligations. The answer is one sentence: "Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever." It opens a little book of questions called the Westminster Shorter Catechism, which Presbyterian and other Reformed churches use to teach the faith. This path met that sentence once before, in passing. Today it gets a whole day. Today's word: the chief end.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CHIEF END OF MAN?`

segments.voice: Start with the word end. Here it doesn't mean the finish line. It means the purpose, the thing something is for, the way a key is for opening a door. So the question is: what is a person for? Now look at the answer's grammar. Glorify, and enjoy. Two verbs, but one end, singular. The catechism doesn't say a life has a serious purpose and then, separately, a pleasant one. It joins them with a single and. To give God glory and to delight in God are, in this sentence, one thing. Then two words at the close: for ever. Not only on good days. This is where the sentence meets the hard questions of these last weeks. The catechism backs its answers with scripture, and one passage given here is Psalm seventy-three. That psalm gives one line to God's goodness, then turns straight to a man who nearly gave up: "my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped." He watched cruel people do well and good people suffer, and it was "too painful for me." Until he went into the sanctuary of God. And then he says: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee." And then, still honest: "My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever." His body failing, his heart failing, and still, enjoyment of God. Paul brings the same end down to the kitchen table: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Eating and drinking. A whole teaching about God, and the first answer has the word enjoy in it.
screen: `EAT, OR DRINK: TO THE GLORY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enjoy God in one thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose one small thing within reach: the warmth of a cup, light on a wall, the taste of whatever you last ate, the sound of someone in the next room. Don't analyze it. Stay with it until it is simply good to you. If you pray, you can let that enjoyment be your thanks, without adding words. If you don't, let the small thing be enough for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The chief end. In the Westminster Shorter Catechism, what a human life is for: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. One end, with two verbs.

Your line: glorify and enjoy. Today, at one ordinary meal or drink, slow down for the first mouthful and let it be good. Paul put eating and drinking on the list. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In Presbyterian and other Reformed churches, children and new members can learn the Westminster Shorter Catechism by question and answer, starting from this first question.

myth: in the catechism, end means the end of your life
it means purpose: what a person is for.
the answer gives a life two separate ends, one serious and one pleasant
it names one end, with two verbs joined by a single and: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.
in Psalm 73, the singer nearly gives up before he calls God his portion
"my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped." only later does he say God is his portion for ever.

fork.setup: you're the singer of Psalm 73. you've watched cruel people do well and good people suffer, and it's too painful to understand. what do you do?
options: go into the sanctuary of God.
quit, and decide it was all for nothing.
go and argue it out with the cruel people.
fork.reveal: he goes into the sanctuary of God, and ends up saying: "whom have I in heaven but thee?" the joy comes after the slipping, not instead of it.

original.note: Greek: glory, the word in Paul's line, do all to the glory of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a catechism is a list of rules to memorize.
what it means: its first question asks what a life is for, and the answer ends in joy: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.
what a scholar hears: one end, two verbs. the catechism backs the answer with scripture, including Psalm 73, where joy in God comes after nearly giving up.

notes: The catechism's date (1647, in the index title) is not repeated in the voice under the claims rule. Confirm the wording of Q1 as quoted (some editions print 'for ever', some 'forever').

The script says the catechism backs Q1 with scripture including Psalm 73 and 1 Corinthians 10:31; the standard proof texts for Q1 are usually given as 1 Cor 10:31, Rom 11:36, Ps 73:24–28 and John 17:21–23. Confirm.
'still taught in Presbyterian churches' and 'written for Reformed churches in England and Scotland' — confirm phrasing.
'Christians who learned this catechism as children sometimes say the second verb surprised them most' is a soft anecdotal claim; Keeper may prefer to cut it.
Day 290 quoted Q1 in passing (Lutherans and the Reformed); the hook acknowledges that. This day takes a new angle (one end, two verbs; Psalm 73 within Block G).

Audit pass: Psalm 73 does not 'start' with the man who nearly gave up (73:1 is 'Truly God is good to Israel'; the slipping is 73:2), so the teach and myth now say it turns there after one line; fixed the garbled key/end image; fork answer moved off position 1 (every nearby fork used it).

Editor pass: cut 'the plain English of its century' (implied date) and the unsourced anecdote that learners found 'enjoy' the most surprising verb; softened the catechism's origin/usage line and howItsDone to avoid unsourced history and 'often' claims.
